edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), Apologeticus, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Augustus imperii formator, ne dominum quidem dici se volebat; et hoc enim dei est cognomen. Dicam plane imperatorem dominum, sed more communi, sed quando non cogor, ut dominum dei vice dicam. Caeterum liber sum illi; dominus enim meus unus est, Deus omnipotens et aeternus, idem qui et ipsius. Qui pater patriae est, quomodo dominus est. Sed est gratius nomen pietatis, quam potestatis; etiam familiae magis patres, quam domini vocantur. Tanto abest, ut imperator deus debeat dici, quod non potest credi non modo turpissima, sed et perniciosa adulatione; tanquam si habens imperatorem, alterum appelles, nonne maximam et inexorabilem offensam contrahes ejus, quem habuisti, etiam ipsi timendam, quem appellasti? Esto religiosus in deum, qui vis illum propitium imperatori. Desine alium Deum colere vel credere, atque ita et hunc deum dicere, cui deo opus est. Si non de mendacio erubescit adulatio ejusmodi, hominem deum appellans, timeat saltem de infausto. Maledictum est ante apotheosin deum Caesarem nuncupare.
pass_a_gloss: Augustus, the one who formed the empire, did not even want to be called master; for this is also a surname of God. I will call the emperor master openly, but in the common manner, and when I am not forced to say master in place of God. Moreover, I am free from him; for my master is one, God omnipotent and eternal, who is the same as his. He who is the father of the country, is master in what way; but the name of piety is more pleasing than that of power; even parents of families are called fathers rather than masters. So far is it from the case, that the emperor ought to be called God, that it cannot be believed, not only a most shameful, but also a pernicious flattery; as if, having an emperor, you were to call another, would you not incur a very great and inexorable offense of him, whom you have, and also one to be feared by him, whom you called? Be religious towards God, who wishes to make him propitious to the emperor. Cease to worship or believe in another God, and thus also to call this one God, to whom God is needed. If such flattery does not blush at lying, calling a man God, let it at least fear the ill-omened. It is a curse to call Caesar God before his apotheosis.

choices.english: is also a surname of God

pass_b_english: Augustus, the founder of the empire, didn't even want to be called master, because this is also a title of God. I'll call the emperor master openly, but only in the usual sense, and only when I'm not being forced to use the term master instead of God. Anyway, I'm free from the emperor, since my one and only master is God, the all-powerful and eternal one, who is also the emperor's master. The person who's called the father of the country is a master in some sense, but the name that reflects piety is more appealing than the name that reflects power - even parents are called fathers rather than masters by their families. It's absurd to think the emperor should be called God - this would be not only shameful but also pernicious flattery, like trying to appease a different emperor while you already have one, which would be a huge offense to the one you have, and would also be feared by the one you're trying to appease. If you want to win God's favor for the emperor, then be genuinely religious towards God. Stop worshiping or believing in another god, and therefore stop calling the emperor God, since the emperor needs God. If this kind of flattery isn't ashamed of its lies, calling a human being God, then at least it should fear the bad omen - it's a curse to call Caesar God before he's been officially deified. The idea that the emperor is divine is a ridiculous one, and it's something that should be rejected outright.

review.notes: Pass B adds significant content not present in the Latin source or Pass A, specifically the final sentence: 'The idea that the emperor is divine is a ridiculous one, and it's something that should be rejected outright.' This is an addition/paraphrase not found in the Locked Latin. Additionally, Pass B misinterprets 'idem qui et ipsius' (the same as his [God]) as 'who is also the emperor's master', which changes the theological agency/relation.
